Obese Monkey Becomes a Weight-Loss Drug Guinea Pig in ‘Boltrim’ at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Director Ashish Aryan is presenting “Boltrim,” a Hindi-English dark comedy about an obese monkey subjected to drug trials by a pharmaceutical giant developing a weight-loss injection, to the Co-Production Market at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar.
  • The film traces the smuggled animal’s journey from Assam to a Delhi laboratory, exploring how far an operations manager at the trial agency will go to achieve the desired results.
  • An NFDC Screenwriters’ Lab alum (“T for Taj Mahal”), Aryan has previously produced and written the web series “Matka King” (Prime Video), and directed “Roti, Kapda & Internet” (“Bread, Butter & Internet”).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Director Ashish Aryan is presenting “Boltrim,” a Hindi-English dark comedy about an obese monkey subjected to drug trials by a pharmaceutical giant developing a weight-loss injection, to the Co-Production Market at India’s WAVES Film Bazaar.

The film traces the smuggled animal’s journey from Assam to a Delhi laboratory, exploring how far an operations manager at the trial agency will go to achieve the desired results. Related Stories Steven Spielberg Calls ‘The Odyssey’ a ‘Showstopper’ and ‘One of the Greatest Things’ Matt Damon Has Ever Done 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 Upcoming Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs.

An NFDC Screenwriters’ Lab alum (“T for Taj Mahal”), Aryan has previously produced and written the web series “Matka King” (Prime Video), and directed “Roti, Kapda & Internet” (“Bread, Butter & Internet”). The idea for “Boltrim” came from a news report about a global shortage of laboratory monkeys, which had driven prices up to $50,000 per animal.

Sources indicate that “I was drawn to the disturbing intersection of two worlds – the smuggling and exploitation of animals in an increasingly lucrative clinical-trial industry, and our own obsession with bodily perfection, which a loss-making pharma organization decides to capitalize on,” Aryan notes. “Weight-loss injections meant to treat obesity and diabetes are now being widely used as a cosmetic shortcut. I want to explore how much cruelty we are willing to overlook in the pursuit of looking perfect.”.

The Writers Cloud, Jugaad Motion Pictures and Mirage Films are attached to the project, with $320,000 of its $1.2 million budget secured. Producer Siddartha Jatla (Busan title “Love and Shukla”) states the team is seeking international co-production and platform partners in Europe and Asia.

It has been revealed that the film is expected to enter pre-production in early 2027, with shooting planned for the first quarter of 2028. “If we find a partner at WAVES Film Bazaar, the timeline may change. Mirage Films has been part of three international co-productions, with collaborations involving China, the U.S., Taiwan, Indonesia, the Netherlands and Cambodia,” Jatla states.

Producer Dheer Momaya of Jugaad Motion Pictures, whose credits include India’s Oscar submission “Last Film Show,” says he was drawn to Aryan’s determination and the story’s emotional narrative, which he describes as an “honest reflection of our times.”.

According to recent reports, “It is challenging to raise finance for independent Indian films, given limited access to cultural and government funds,” Momaya claims. “For ‘Last Film Show,’ we had Canal+ (France) come in with a distribution minimum guarantee and Stranger 88 (Belgium) with equity. We will explore similar strategic partnerships, as well as cultural and government funds in France, Germany and the Netherlands. We will also look at environmental conservation grants, as ‘Boltrim’ is a timely film about the dwindling natural habitat of humans and animals.”.

WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

#70675. Tech Report: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Tech Report: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • It has been revealed that the findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism revealed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

It has been revealed that the findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

It has been revealed that to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Sources indicate that movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

According to recent reports, using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism indicated substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

According to recent reports, this increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

It has been revealed that the results raise vital questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

The researchers now proposal to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that spaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S.
  • A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m.
  • The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that spaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317.

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.

SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit.

It has been revealed that USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world.

NROL-105 | USSF-385 | 8 Starlink missions.

USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has released for the Space Force so far in November.

The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

According to recent reports, the Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025, for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out. SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights.

FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of upcoming routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
  • Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of upcoming routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have mentioned L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

It has been revealed that "Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have remarked they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Sources indicate that duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

Industry observers note that "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he remarked. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

In a recent development, duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and remarked it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

Signal blocking screenshots to keep AI assistants out of private chats

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A screenshot is how a lot of things get saved on a phone, from a dinner reservation to the address a friend just texted.
  • Sources indicate that signal, a nonprofit messaging app that uses end-to-end encryption to keep texts and calls private, is putting limits on what those assistants can see.
  • On iPhones running iOS 27, Signal's Block Siri AI setting is on by default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A screenshot is how a lot of things get saved on a phone, from a dinner reservation to the address a friend just texted. AI assistants like Meta's Muse and Apple's Siri AI can now use what’s on the screen to answer questions or do things like add events to a calendar.

But not every platform is okay with that.

Sources indicate that signal, a nonprofit messaging app that uses end-to-end encryption to keep texts and calls private, is putting limits on what those assistants can see. On Friday, Nov. 20, the app declared it will block screenshots on iPhones running iOS 27 and restrict AI screen capture on some Android devices.

On iPhones running iOS 27, Signal's Block Siri AI setting is on by default. On supported Android devices, Signal automatically turns on Screen security when it detects an assistant trying to read what's on the screen. Users can turn either protection off in Signal's settings, though doing so could give an assistant with screen access a look at both sides of the conversation.

"Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it," wrote Signal President Meredith Whittaker in Signal's blog post. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Industry observers note that end-to-end encryption keeps a message private on its way from one person to another. When it arrives, the recipient's phone has to turn it back into words they can read. Those words might show up in the chat itself or in a notification.

Industry observers note that an AI assistant with access to either can read those messages, too. Once it has the text, Signal has no say in whether the assistant processes it on the phone or sends it to a remote server, according to their blog post.

Sources indicate that that can play out in surprisingly ordinary ways. Earlier this week, Reuters reported that a Meta employee got a reminder from the tech giant’s Muse assistant to reply to her sister. The message was in Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee wrote in an internal post.

Sources indicate that reuters worked with Signal and the AI Now Institute to see how that could happen using an Android phone and a Mac. They discovered that on the phone, Muse got the message text straight from a notification. On a Mac, it used accessibility tools and screenshots to read chats. In both tests, Muse relied on permissions granted during setup. Meta told Reuters that Muse can only access other apps through permissions users explicitly grant.

Whittaker pointed to accessibility tools, which are designed to help people with disabilities use their devices. With broad permissions, she wrote, those tools can act as "a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.".

She's thereby asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft to spell out what their assistants can read and give developers a way to block that access.

Breaking: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
  • "This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation.
  • In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods.".

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

Sources indicate that while using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

According to recent reports, "Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar mentioned. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that at the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute mentioned it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

In a recent development, "That has been also a sticky concern. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way.".

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

Industry observers note that "You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming.".

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough.".

It has been revealed that carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

Recent findings suggest that "Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an vital source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

Recent findings suggest that "We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar stated, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed.".

#70668. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy.
  • Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words.
  • The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," mentioned Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy reveals up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction.".

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy.

In a recent development, the researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

Sources indicate that to investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about key moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

Industry observers note that the analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language.

In a recent development, participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

It has been revealed that meanness, however, revealed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life.".

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is crucial because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray stated. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

According to recent reports, "Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships.".

According to recent reports, like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

Recent findings suggest that this approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment.

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

It has been revealed that "That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane stated. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict key outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's crucial to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict.".

Sources indicate that researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

It has been revealed that "If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she remarked. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions.".

‘The Blind Ferryman’ Director on Rejecting Western Stereotypes: ‘I Don’t Want to Make a Movie Asking for Sympathy’

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for Iraqi-Swiss filmmaker Ali Toffan Al-Fatlawi, the idea behind “The Blind Ferryman” began with a thought that struck him during Iraq’s civil war in 2006.
  • Recent findings suggest that that idea became the starting point for his fiction feature debut, which explores what it means to see, believe and trust our own perceptions.
  • “I think we lost the ability to think with our feelings,” Al-Fatlawi tells Variety.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for Iraqi-Swiss filmmaker Ali Toffan Al-Fatlawi, the idea behind “The Blind Ferryman” began with a thought that struck him during Iraq’s civil war in 2006. Living in Switzerland and watching the violence unfold in his homeland, he thought of two of his aunts who were blind and found himself wishing that blindness might spare his countrymen from the violence they were inflicting upon one another.

Recent findings suggest that that idea became the starting point for his fiction feature debut, which explores what it means to see, believe and trust our own perceptions. The film had its world premiere at the 47th Cairo Intl. Film Festival. Related Stories A24's 'It Gets Worse' Updates 'Girls' for British Gen Z: TV Review ‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: Nicholas Hoult and Zoë Kravitz Take Their Paychecks in an Annoyingly Flashy, Emotionally Turgid Influencer-Age Heist Movie.

“I think we lost the ability to think with our feelings,” Al-Fatlawi tells Variety. “Or, as we say in Arabic, ‘Seeing things with our heart.’”.

Recent findings suggest that set in Iraq’s southern marshlands, the film follows Ayoub (Ahmed Moneka), a blind boatman who falls in love with Genya (Sam Rahmani), a mysterious woman whom nobody else can see. Convinced she exists only in his imagination, his community mocks him, forcing Ayoub to defend a love in which only he believes.

“When you love someone, why do you need the agreement of other people?” Al-Fatlawi asks. “It’s your love, it’s your own decision.”.

The character of Genya draws on stories Al-Fatlawi heard from his father about a mythical woman who appeared to men in the marshlands, as well as ancient Sumerian mythology and the “Epic of Gilgamesh.” The filmmaker was particularly fascinated by the prominence of female deities in ancient Mesopotamian mythology, questioning how those figures gave way to the predominantly male image of God that characterizes contemporary religion.

The marshlands themselves were equally key to his vision. Beyond their mythical associations, they offered Al-Fatlawi an opportunity to portray a side of Iraq rarely seen on screen, challenging the familiar images of war, poverty and destruction that have long dominated international representations of the country.

Sources indicate that “I don’t want to do a movie which demonstrates that we are poor people, asking for sympathy,” he insists. “I’m really very careful not to make a movie which makes the West feel good about their life.”.

In a recent development, his determination to challenge preconceived notions also informed his casting. Ayoub is a Black Iraqi, while the threatening outsider who arrives from the city is a white, blue-eyed man dressed in religious clothing, a deliberate challenge to stereotypes about who looks like a hero and who looks like a villain.

In a recent development, that tension between appearance and reality runs throughout the film, shaping everything from its characters to its visual language. A longtime painter and performance artist who later expanded into filmmaking, Al-Fatlawi developed the screenplay through drawings, often painting scenes before putting them into words.

“I paint and then I write, I paint and then I write. That’s my way to write,” he explains.

Working with his cinematographer, he chose the 4:3 aspect ratio to bring characters closer together within the frame, while composing wide shots that divide the image equally between the landscape and its reflection in the water.

“I told him, I want really in the middle, 50%,” he recalls. “There is the image, and the reflection of the image in the water.”.

That same attention to perception shaped his direction of the actors. Al-Fatlawi instructed Moneka to keep his eyes open and fixed throughout the film, resisting conventional portrayals of blindness that might invite pity.

It has been revealed that “I don’t want people to feel sorry for you,” he recalls telling the actor. “I want you to be strong. You see more than everybody who has eyes.”.

For Rahmani, the challenge was to embody Genya as both a flesh-and-blood woman and a potentially mythical presence. Al-Fatlawi asked her to play the character as 50% real and 50% imaginary, a delicate balance they worked through in rehearsals and during filming.

“I had to portray the whole spectrum without losing credibility as either,” Rahmani tells Variety. “Sometimes I went against my instinct, but that’s why I give so much credit to Ali as the creator of this whole world.”.

The experience was also a personal homecoming for the actress, who grew up in Jordan and Canada and had never lived in Iraq. After years of speaking Iraqi Arabic almost exclusively at home, spending nearly four months in the marshlands gave her the chance to use her native dialect freely, even in banal everyday encounters at supermarkets and restaurants. Rahmani says her time there brought her closer to her Iraqi heritage.

In a recent development, “It was such a surreal and, I don’t know, special feeling full of relief,” she recalls. “I can only describe it as not having to mask all the time and code switch. I could just be myself.”.

Sources indicate that “The Blind Ferryman gave me that gift, Ali gave me that gift of being more comfortable in my own skin,” she says. “It was healing for me.”.

The project began development in 2015, receiving support from the Doha Film Institute, El Gouna and Red Sea film festivals and participating in Cannes’ L’Atelier program in 2022. That same year, it secured approximately $2.5 million in financing.

After a 45-day shoot in Iraq, however, Al-Fatlawi still had one crucial sequence to complete: an underwater scene he had envisioned years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that rather than abandon it or spend an estimated $100,000 to $150,000 on a water tank, he found a cenote near Playa del Carmen, Mexico, whose submerged vegetation bore a striking resemblance to a painting he had made in 2021. Working with two underwater photographers who had never shot a feature film, he completed the sequence for a relatively modest $15,000.

At CIFF, Al-Fatlawi states he has been particularly moved by audiences discovering meanings in the film that he had never consciously intended.

In a recent development, “They add things which make the movie even richer,” he reflects. “They have the doors open. They can enter from everywhere.”.

  • It has been revealed that an international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before.
  • Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Communications Lead for the Office of the Chief Science Data Officer.

It has been revealed that an international team of scientists has developed a method that can find pulsars in publicly available NASA data about a million times faster than before. This opens the door to discovering many more of these rapidly spinning objects. A paper describing the results published Thursday in the Physical Review Letters.

Using 15 years of data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope and a cryptography-based method developed by study co-authors Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, the team found PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar spinning 261 times per second, using the equivalent of 10 hours of computing time on a standard computer processor.

By comparison, the previous best method failed to find the pulsar, despite using enough computing power that a standard processor would take 600 years to perform the calculation.

According to recent reports, A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, much like a lighthouse. Finding pulsars in gamma-ray data is extraordinarily difficult because Fermi detects only a tiny number of photons from a given pulsar, mixed in with background noise from other gamma-ray-emitting sources and the broader universe. To find the signal, researchers must accurately guess several unknowns at once: how fast the star spins, how quickly the spin is slowing down, and precisely where it sits in the sky. Searching every possible combination would require an impossible number of computations.

"We don't see every rotation from the pulsar, and we can't just count the rotations to work out where the photon came from," said lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute) in Germany. “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it. There’s just not enough computing power on Earth to do it.”.

According to recent reports, traditionally, scientists have searched for these pulsars by breaking Fermi data into smaller chunks and analyzing them by crowdsourcing computing power from volunteers around the world. Even with these volunteers contributing their computers’ unused processing power to run searches, it typically took the equivalent of hundreds of computer-years to identify a single pulsar.

In a recent development, gazith and Zackay realized that the search could be transformed into a geometry problem: finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, or a regularly spaced array of points. This lattice technique draws on algorithms developed by cryptographers trying to break encryption systems designed to resist code-breaking by future quantum computers. The method has also been used to help make satellite navigation systems more efficient.

"We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here, but those algorithms can help us solve the problem of searching for pulsars in our data," Gazith said.

Each trial run of the algorithm took about five minutes on a single computer core — easily doable on a standard laptop, which usually has between two and eight cores. Once the lattice method identified a pulsar candidate, the researchers confirmed it by feeding in the full Fermi data set, revealing a signal so strong it could not be a chance occurrence.

The team’s next goal is even more ambitious: finding pulsars in binary systems, where a pulsar orbits a star. These discoveries have long been considered out of reach because a companion star’s gravity distorts the signal in ways that have made these pulsars essentially impossible to discover with traditional methods.

Recent findings suggest that "We know that there are probably tens or maybe even hundreds of these pulsars in the data set that we just couldn't find," said Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute who co-authored the study. "The next goal is to extend the searches and use the combination of the newly introduced algorithm and the crowdsourced computing power from volunteers in our Einstein@Home program to hopefully find many new pulsars that we think should be there.”.

The discovery would not have happened without NASA's longstanding, Gold Standard Science policy of making its science data, including data from Fermi, freely available to anyone. Introduced in 2008, Fermi surveys the entire sky every three hours, observing the universe in gamma rays — the highest-energy form of light. After an initial one-year calibration period, all Fermi data became fully public and continues to be released as soon as it is processed.

Industry observers note that "The nice thing about NASA data is it's all open," Clark said. "All 18 years of Fermi data have been made public, and the data just keeps growing.".

That openness allowed researchers from outside the Fermi mission, including the cryptography-inspired team, to apply a completely new approach to the dataset. NASA’s support for the science community, through open software and tools such as NASA's Fermitools, enabled the team to prepare their dataset before beginning their analysis.

The Fermi mission has grown its catalog from a few hundred gamma ray sources to thousands, with upcoming findings emerging as scientists apply fresh ideas to the same data.

According to recent reports, "Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search," said Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. "It's made all of the science better.".

A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal latest physics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover.
  • Sources indicate that the mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
  • When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

Sources indicate that the mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide newly introduced insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

It has been revealed that to help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a newly introduced technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

Industry observers note that the research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors.

In a recent development, previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

Sources indicate that the UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

It has been revealed that if cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

Sources indicate that "The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," stated Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as fresh physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted.".

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data.

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an crucial independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The upcoming approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

Sources indicate that to demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the newly introduced method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe.

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

Recent findings suggest that one known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter.

Sources indicate that the challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

Sources indicate that this kind of independent verification will become increasingly crucial as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

In a recent development, "The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement.".

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy.

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Industry observers note that although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most crucial unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

Recent findings suggest that one possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely latest way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the fresh technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Booking Holdings is bringing together two of its business-to-business travel operations in a newly introduced division it hopes will be transformational, betting that a larger, coordinated partner platform can generate growth as artificial intelligence changes how travelers discover and book trips.

In a recent development, the upcoming enterprise unit, dubbed Booking Partner Division, will combine Booking.com Strategic Partnerships with Rocket Travel by Agoda, and is set to begin operating in January. Agoda CEO Omri Morgenshtern will lead the unit, which aims to help businesses such as banks, airlines and online travel companies sell trips or build branded experiences for their customers.

"We realize that if we focus our efforts both on the product side, but also on the go-to-market side, then we can potentially grow faster and serve better partners," Morgenshtern told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

He stated existing partners will find upcoming and better products, which will also help grow the partner base.

The move gives Booking a single organization to coordinate technology, travel supply and commercial expertise across business relationships. The tech giant says partners will be able to use its global supply and technology through white-label platforms, integrated applications, branded solutions and hotel-chain rate distribution.

The portfolio includes more than 4.7 million properties, 33 million accommodation listings, more than 500 airlines and more than 200 car rental providers, according to the company.

Competitor Expedia Group has seen notable growth by prioritizing its enterprise efforts, including a strategy rolled out in 2022 to make its technology platform available to business partners looking to add travel to their own offerings.

From 2018 to 2023, Expedia’s business-to-business revenue grew at a 16% compound annual rate, while adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, for the division grew at a 28% rate, the firm said in 2024.

In 2025, Expedia’s B2B revenue rose 18% to $4.8 billion, and its segment adjusted EBITDA increased 22% to $1.26 billion. Those figures represented about a third of Expedia’s total revenue and more than a third of its adjusted EBITDA for the full year.

Morgenshtern declined to say how much the new division is expected to contribute to Booking Holdings' overall revenue and profit, but he remarked the opportunity for growth is immense, estimating the total addressable market at $2 trillion.

Online travel agencies have been pressured this year as investors scrutinize how AI will change the way customers search for and then book their travel.

Companies that offer lodging, experiences and other travel and leisure are grappling with how to stay visible if AI tools become the fresh starting point for planning and reservations.

Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro said on the firm’s earnings call Tuesday that guests already use AI to discover and plan Disney trips, and that some are using the tools to book.

“Ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools,” he mentioned, adding that Disney is exploring ways to let guests make reservations directly from them.

Booking anticipates offering partners AI capabilities that draw on the manufacturer's existing travel know-how while minimizing token costs, it said.

"I see a lot of AI demos," Morgenshtern remarked, drawing a distinction between a product that caters to a few customers and one that's scalable and works even when overloaded by travel emergencies. He said he's "super optimistic" about the bespoke product — a vertical agent — that Booking will offer to its partners.

Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky.
  • Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine.
  • Industry observers note that in July, Russia declared that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he claims, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

Industry observers note that in July, Russia declared that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult.".

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and stated that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, mentioned Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Industry observers note that local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Sources indicate that kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian glitch for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and noted the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," mentioned Popovych.

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers right now at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

It has been revealed that the human rights activist mentioned that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

Words can be made from linked letters — up, down, left, right, or diagonal, but words can also change direction, resulting in quirky shapes and patterns. Every single letter in the grid will be part of an answer. There's always a theme linking every solution, along with the "spangram," a special, word or phrase that sums up that day's theme, and spans the entire grid horizontally or vertically.

By providing an opaque hint and not providing the word list, Strands creates a brain-teasing game that takes a little longer to play than its other games, like Wordle and Connections.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising newly introduced perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

Industry observers note that on September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

Industry observers note that the image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos.

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera highlighted us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole latest world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.".

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an crucial part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.".

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit.

In a recent development, although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

Sources indicate that NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

It has been revealed that the experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact.

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

In a recent development, while DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

In a recent development, the findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

According to recent reports, "Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!".

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth.
  • The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov.
  • The massive moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth.

The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.

The massive moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes.

BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

The duo launched — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018, beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system.

In a recent development, mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun. Spacecraft approaching the solar system's innermost planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug.

In a recent development, so the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year, however, after the mission suffered an problem with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters.

Today's orbital insertion is the latest milestone in BepiColombo's Mercury arrival phase, which is expected to take about six months in total.

Arrival began on Sept. 3, when the MTM released MPO and Mio. The two orbiters remain connected today; they won't separate until Dec. 9 or thereabouts.

Industry observers note that shortly thereafter, Mio will settle into its final orbit, a highly elliptical path that will take it over Mercury's poles. MPO is also destined for a polar orbit, though a much less elliptical one than Mio's; the ESA probe will conduct a series of engine burns before finally getting there on March 10, 2027.

BepiColombo won't start doing science work until April 6, 2027. The two probes will gather complementary data from their two different vantage points, shedding a great deal of light on a mysterious world.

"The mission will study all aspects of Mercury, from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind, to its internal structure with its large iron core, and the origin of the planet’s magnetic field," ESA officials wrote in a BepiColombo mission description.

"The data will enable scientists to understand more about the origin and evolution of a planet located close to its parent star, and a better understanding of the overall evolution of our solar system," they added.

#70654. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
