New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency.
  • Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an notable clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature.
  • To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an notable clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising newly introduced direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

It has been revealed that that resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an vital advance.

It has been revealed that however, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," indicates Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced study provides an key piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

According to recent reports, "This is really good news," claims Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The fresh findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

According to recent reports, "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

Recent findings suggest that phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Recent findings suggest that unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the manufacturer said it saw strength among professional shoppers.

It has been revealed that the tech giant noted comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

It has been revealed that because of the strength, Lowe's now remarked it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

Sources indicate that CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the firm is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He remarked Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

Industry observers note that lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the firm plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

"We are giving those pros what they need," he remarked. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program.".

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

It has been revealed that for the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

Industry observers note that the home improvement retailer has previously noted it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The organization is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives remarked on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the organization remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot remarked earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a fresh explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but fresh research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a fresh explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he stated.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Sources indicate that yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

Recent findings suggest that one of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

Industry observers note that the amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

Recent findings suggest that the mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to recent reports, according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Latest Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly notable finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

According to recent reports, "Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament mentioned.

In a recent development, the research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

Recent findings suggest that "Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific.
  • According to recent reports, named Xavier, the system intensified rapidly, thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tropical Cyclone Xavier launched the basin’s storm season with a bang.

In a recent development, even as the unusually quiet 2026 storm season winds down in the North Atlantic, seas have begun to stir on the other side of the world in the Southwest Pacific. On November 15, 2026, the Fiji Meteorological Service began issuing updates about a slow-moving tropical disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands. Within just a few days, it had become one of the most intense November tropical cyclones the region has seen in decades.

According to recent reports, named Xavier, the system intensified rapidly, thriving in an environment with minimal wind shear and sea surface temperatures of 29 degrees Celsius (84 degrees Fahrenheit)—well above the threshold required to sustain and strengthen developing tropical cyclones. Xavier was the basin’s second named storm of the season, following only Wati, a short-lived storm that emerged in October.

As Xavier developed, NASA satellite data showed the storm churning along the southwestern edge of a massive tongue of warm water spanning from the west coast of South America to the central Pacific—a telltale sign of the El Niño that has been present in the region since June.

Industry observers note that when the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this image at 02:53 Universal Time on November 17, 2026 (4:53 p.m. Cook Islands Time on November 16), forecasters estimated Xavier had maximum winds of about 195 kilometers (120 miles) per hour. Winds reached a peak intensity of 220 kilometers (140 miles) per hour later that day, a Category 5 storm on the cyclone intensity scale used in the region or a Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale.

It has been revealed that the storm ranks as the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the international date line on record, noted Colorado State University hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach. Xavier’s formation east of the date line, near the northern Cook Islands, was unusual, but its easterly position aligns with research that indicates that storm activity in the region typically shifts northeast during El Niño years. Research also shows that El Niño tends to fuel storms that strengthen at an unusually rapid pace.

In a recent development, according to news reports, Xavier damaged homes and caused power disruptions as it passed the northern Cook Islands. It then encountered dry air and a less favorable wind shear environment and slowly weakened as it pushed westward, reducing the threat that it posed to Samoa and American Samoa.

Industry observers note that xavier is likely one of the first of several storms to affect the region in the coming months. A seasonal outlook from the Fiji Meteorological Service projects that the region could see between 11 and 15 named tropical cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the international date line. Storm activity in the Southwest Pacific basin typically peaks in February.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games has unveiled, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.
  • Industry observers note that the worldwide figure was based on organization estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game rolled out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time.

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games has unveiled, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.

Industry observers note that the worldwide figure was based on organization estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game rolled out. Rockstar stated also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement.

The company stated the sales set “a fresh record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”.

The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013.

It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar.

The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.

The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.

Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.

Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.

Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.

Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved.

While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.

With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

According to recent reports, there is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.

The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.

“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”.

With the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse.

Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A newly introduced study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A newly introduced study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

Measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

New Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

In a recent development, for generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, stated:.

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each upcoming piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

Recent findings suggest that if the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

In a recent development, "In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as vital as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

It has been revealed that the international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

According to recent reports, and that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

Industry observers note that the impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

According to recent reports, "It feels like your eyes are burning," mentioned Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven.".

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, indicates Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.

The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker states limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that failure to cut emissions swiftly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today.".

He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

According to recent reports, but no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system.".

Industry observers note that france is sticking to a previously unveiled deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

According to recent reports, germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

According to recent reports, "None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition proposal.".

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

Industry observers note that and it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she mentioned. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

Industry observers note that that vehicle, known as Ship 42, introduced Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who mentioned it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

Recent findings suggest that "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk noted on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship introduces to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.).

Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.).

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the organization had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has remarked that the tech giant wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Sources indicate that assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which debuted on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory are read V-G-R. That's a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft presently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away. How long did it take the message to reach humanity's most distant interstellar spacecraft? Traveling at the speed of light, the answer is one day. In fact, the Voyager 1 spacecraft was confirmed to reach its one light-day distance milestone on November 18, at 10:16:07 UTC, nearly 50 years after launch in 1977. For extra credit, fans of math can calculate that at one light-day per 50 years, Voyager 1 will reach its one light-year (365 light-days) distance milestone in about 18,250 years.Tomorrow's picture: cruising.

Industry News: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard.
  • Recent findings suggest that members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Recent findings suggest that members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

Recent findings suggest that "Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," mentioned Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, the discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

In a recent development, rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

The clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

Scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

The team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

"Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," said Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

Sources indicate that the rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

Recent findings suggest that MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two vital firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the fresh flagship research vessel David Packard.

In a recent development, MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you look up at the sky tonight, you'll notice the Moon is looking noticeably fuller than it did earlier in the week. We're still in the Waxing Gibbous phase, which falls between the First Quarter and Full Moon, but we're getting closer to the Full Moon every night.

Recent findings suggest that as of Saturday, Nov. 21, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 85% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Imbrium and Vaporum, as well as the Kepler Crater. With binoculars, you'll also see the Mare Frigoris, the Clavius Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 15 and 17 landing spots, and the Rima Hyginus.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

In a recent development, according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a New Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

Upcoming Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

It has been revealed that first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

According to recent reports, waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Did Democrats fail Florida? Angie Nixon on ‘missed opportunity’ in midterms

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1349 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The party invested in key battlegrounds, netting stunning wins at the expense of candidates in Florida and Louisiana.
  • To call it a blue wave, stated the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, would be an epic understatement.
  • On a night when almost everything else went right for Democrats, David Jolly fell short by 1.3 percentage points against Republican Byron Donalds, who will become Florida’s first Black governor, while Angie Nixon, bidding to become the state’s first Black senator, lost by 2.9 percentage points to Republican Ashley Moody.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The party invested in key battlegrounds, netting stunning wins at the expense of candidates in Florida and Louisiana.

To call it a blue wave, stated the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, would be an epic understatement. The midterm elections were “the political equivalent of a meteor strike”. But one state, DeSantis added with pride, was able to “hold the line”. And that state was Florida.

On a night when almost everything else went right for Democrats, David Jolly fell short by 1.3 percentage points against Republican Byron Donalds, who will become Florida’s first Black governor, while Angie Nixon, bidding to become the state’s first Black senator, lost by 2.9 percentage points to Republican Ashley Moody.

According to recent reports, even the losses, however, were remarkable performances in a state that has shifted right in recent years and become the adopted home of Donald Trump, and where two years ago he defeated Kamala Harris by 13 percentage points. In an election where Democrats were winning in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, Nixon was left asking: did Florida Democrats lose because the party didn’t support them?

According to recent reports, “It was a missed opportunity,” the 42-year-old mentioned pointedly. “I’m going to work to bring everybody together so that we don’t miss opportunities like that anymore.”.

Sources indicate that democratic party leaders and major national donors made calculated investments in key battlegrounds elsewhere, producing stunning victories in unexpected places. Yet that generosity came at the expense of southern states like Florida and Louisiana, where local candidates were largely left to fend for themselves.

Sources indicate that was that because too many people had written Florida off as a red state? “Folks often write the south off. Now we’ve shown that Florida is in play, the south is in play, and I’m hoping that through my advocacy and me being so vocal that people will take note and will listen and donate to more candidates in the south,” Nixon remarked.

According to recent reports, with nearly 24 million people, Florida is the third most populous state in the US. Covering its vast geographical expanse requires a huge war chest and saturation TV strategy. Nixon had neither. “I would say we were out-fundraised and Florida’s a very big state,” was her simple diagnosis.

Moody had raised $14.5m compared to Nixon’s $11.3m, according to the Federal Election Commission, while outside groups spent $10.4m opposing Nixon versus $3.6m spent opposing Moody.

Sources indicate that without the funds to buy airtime across Florida’s multiple expensive media markets – from Miami and Orlando to Tampa and Jacksonville – Nixon found herself overwhelmed by negative advertising from Moody and her allied political committees. “They hit me hard on it, and we didn’t have enough money to push back until it was too late.”.

Recent findings suggest that while conservative groups sought to depict Nixon as a far left extremist (“Angie Nixon is actually a socialist,” said one), she believes it was a more traditional attack that hurt her the most. “Those didn’t necessarily work. What we saw worked was when they were trying to say that I was raising taxes on people.”.

By the time Nixon’s campaign could afford to explain her economic platform, the ads had done their damage. Nixon believes that “of course” national Democrats should have intervened sooner. But she is careful not to dwell too long on the blame game.

“I wish more people gave me money, period. I’m going to work to move forward and work to organise and create an environment where, despite whatever the conditions of that year are, that we’ll still be able to win.”.

Nixon’s optimism is bolstered by what transpired on election night in other southern contests, where underfunded candidates demonstrated that progressive, community centred campaigns can break through longstanding conservative strongholds.

She points to Scott Colom, the progressive prosecutor who became the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era. The lesson of those races, for Nixon, is that no red state is a monolith and no southern state is permanently out of reach if the party is willing to contest it.

In a recent development, even with more money, however, any Democrat running in Florida faces a structural barrier erected over successive legislative sessions: the deliberate erosion of voting rights. Nixon points the finger at DeSantis. “That man has done so much as it relates to voter suppression. He’s done so much to suppress voters. Every single year they have attacked voting rights and the election laws and so now we’re dealing with that.”.

While turnout rates among registered Democrats remained high, the overall playing field has been warped by the fact Florida now has 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, a huge reversal after Democrats held the advantage for decades.

Nixon argues that this gap did not emerge organically but was engineered by targeted legislation designed to debilitate voter registration drives. In recent years, Florida’s Republican supermajorities have enacted onerous penalties and strict restrictions on grassroots civic organisations.

According to recent reports, she continued: “That gap is there because they made it harder for third-party organisations to be able to register voters. Historically, those third-party groups registered more people of colour. That was intentional to make it harder.”.

In a state where vote-by-mail (VBM) had long been a secure and convenient staple used by voters of all political stripes, Republicans also changed the rules to require voters to renew their requests for mail ballots after every general election cycle.

Nixon added: “It was also intentional to change up the vote-by-mail laws because again, low-income working families and people of colour vote by mail more often because they’re working.

Recent findings suggest that “They made it hard for that to happen and so we saw a huge drop. Thousands upon thousands of folks who would normally get VBMs did not get them because they didn’t know about the latest law.”.

In short, does Nixon believe she would have won on a level playing field? “Oh, absolutely, yes,” she replied without hesitation. “I do.”.

According to recent reports, it follows that Nixon refuses to accept that Florida, once a quintessential swing state but where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 2012, is now a lost cause. “We need to work to close the voter registration gap. We need to continue to organise and go meet people where they are.”.

It has been revealed that nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America over the summer, though she acknowledged some disagreements with the organisation. During her campaign she shared stages with the progressive stars senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

According to recent reports, but Nixon continues to resist easy categorisation. “I’m not interested in labels,” she said. “I’m interested in working with whoever wants to work to advance the agenda for working families.”.

That agenda, she believes, is where Democrats can rebuild a working-class coalition that cuts across traditional partisan lines. When asked what the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress should prioritise in Washington, Nixon reels off an ambitious populist legislative platform centred on basic economic security.

It has been revealed that “They need to pass comprehensive healthcare: push for Medicare for All. They need to increase the minimum wage. They need to push for comprehensive and compassionate immigration reform. They also need to hold Donald Trump and his people accountable.”.

Does the Democratic party possess a coherent, compelling vision for the future? “We need more diverse voices in the conversation for us to get there,” Nixon noted candidly. “I don’t think we’re there yet.”.

Industry observers note that whether Nixon herself will launch another bid for elected office remains an open question. For now, her focus is on launching a political action committee, Never Scared, so that whoever steps onto the ballot in the future will not face the same structural headwinds she encountered.

“I am deciding right now. What I am doing is working to create the conditions, create the environment where folks will win whether or not the south gets funded by more historical donors.”.

Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
  • The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. Newly introduced research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a new study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

The scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an notable role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," stated Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

Recent findings suggest that for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

Industry observers note that after the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

In a recent development, in mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This demonstrated that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

In a recent development, the more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

This prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than rapidly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

It has been revealed that however, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

Dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

Another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

In a recent development, this result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

According to recent reports, excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The fresh results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another crucial part of this process.

For recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he currently works as a researcher.

Industry observers note that additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

Recent findings suggest that the team is now participating in a upcoming international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.

Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.

There are some notable differences between each Workspace blueprint – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.

Google offers four different Workspace prepares, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of consumers on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.

Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the initiative you choose, there are some vital differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard looks. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.

According to recent reports, gemini is also a substantial difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.

Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.

Recent findings suggest that standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.

At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this proposal, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.

According to recent reports, most people should use the Standard proposal, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.

Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google revealed that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.

You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.

Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to promptly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.

Industry observers note that flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.

Google Workspace Flows is a latest tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.
