📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that considering the current state of affairs, the best gifts for the women in our lives are the ones that let them mentally clock out for a bit. The world is on fire—literally and figuratively. Plastic is melting onto corals, the measles are back, and just to kick us while we’re down, the girlies can’t even enjoy a Caesar salad or some chips and guac in peace. Some days, I'll catch myself staring at the sky and think, I wish I could hitch a ride to space, but of course, Elon Musk has ruined that fantasy for me, too.

If the woman in your life is exhausted by the headlines, by the slow-motion collapse of democracy, by the sheer audacity of men in power, or perhaps just the overall state of humanity, she deserves a treat. She frankly needs a portal to another reality, but since that's not possible just yet, a temporary escape will have to do.

Here are the best gifts for women surviving the dystopian quest that is 2026. For more thoughtful gift ideas for women, check out Gifts for Moms, Best Graduation Gifts, and Best Stocking Stuffers.

Recent findings suggest that she’s been carrying the weight of the world for far too long. Therabody’s ThermBack LED melts away tension with targeted heat, vibration, LED, and far-infrared therapies. With three heat levels (up to 113 degrees Fahrenheit) and three vibration patterns (low, high, and wave), it stimulates circulation, loosens tight muscles in the lower back, and offers relief when she’s sitting at her desk for eight hours trying not to scream. It also doubles as a soothing heat pad for period cramps. Best of all, it automatically shuts off, so she doesn’t have to worry about turning it off. Check out some other options in our guide to the Best Massagers.

Recent findings suggest that when in doubt, perfume makes a lovely gift. A beautifully bottled eau de parfum inherently feels luxurious, but fragrance is a personal territory, so it’s best to avoid anything too polarizing unless you know her tastes. One safe and elegant bet: Bulgari’s Omnia Amethyste Eau de Parfum. Its soft, floral-woody scent is pleasant to wear year-round on its own or layer with her existing favorites. The composition opens with iris petal and ambrette accords, blooms into iris absolute and Damask rose, then settles into a warm, earthy base of bourbon vanilla and cistus labdanum absolute.

Women are expected to do it all, so why shouldn’t their alarm clocks? The Hatch Sleep Clock is a multitasking marvel. Along with being one of the best sunrise clocks on the market, it’s also a dimmable bedside light, a sound machine, and the first Hatch device to offer contactless sleep tracking. That last bit means she can monitor her slumber without strapping yet another gadget to her body. To unlock Hatch’s full audio library, she’ll need a Hatch+ membership ($6 per month), so I'd spring for at least three months. Consider it an investment in everyone’s well-being when she’s finally getting her beauty sleep.

I absolutely adore Quince’s Mongolian cashmere collection. The Oversized Boyfriend Cardigan is the ultimate wardrobe staple for three out of four seasons. It’s not just perfect for sweata-weatha fall; it’s also cozy for rainy spring days and during the chill of winter. The fisherman rib detailing is uber-coastal, a charming touch to an already flattering and versatile piece. If your giftee is more of a sweatshirt gal, you also can't go wrong with the Fisherman Pullover Hoodie ($120) or the Full-Zip Hoodie ($120).

Recent findings suggest that everyone and their mother has an LED mask these days. If the woman in your life doesn’t, congratulations: You’ve found her gift. Chances are the Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask is already on her wishlist. And if it isn't, she simply hasn’t done enough research. The CryoGlow delivers red, infrared, and blue light, which is everything your face could possibly need short of a dermatologist. Its preset routines live on an attached controller, so there’s no troubleshooting. The real selling point, though, is the under-eye cooling pads, which help reduce puffiness and add a therapeutic element to the experience. I gifted one to my mother, and now she has to actively defend it from her friends.

Sources indicate that get her the Eva Wearable Vibrator. A hands-free clitoral stimulation toy that can be used solo, but is best during penetrative sex. It’s tiny. It’s mighty. It’s hands-free (!!!), made of soft silicone, with three intensity levels. Gift the Eva to your best friend, or to your partner if you want to spice things up, in which case, you’re welcome.

Sources indicate that if I have to feed myself, I want a kitchen appliance that does most of my labor. The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Noir is that appliance. She’s goth. She’s gorgeous. She air-fries, slow-cooks, and bakes with zero complaints. There are 11 preset functions, to be exact. I don’t know what all of them do, and I don’t care, because she knows. I don’t want to think about settings, and with Breville’s Element iQ system, which auto-adjusts temperature for precision cooking, I don’t have to. There’s even an app, which I didn’t download because I’m busy. You can check out more of our Air Fryer picks here.

If she already owns an LED mask, it’s time to give her scalp the same VIP treatment. Red-light therapy isn’t just for pattern baldness; it may also help women experiencing all types of hair thinning and shedding, including postpartum hair loss. It can also help calm the scalp, increase blood flow, and regulate oil production. Reviewer Nena Farrell loves the HigherDose Red Light Hat, which is relatively affordable compared with competitors and looks like an ordinary baseball cap. That means she can take her self-care outside, and no one would ever know. How would they know?

According to recent reports, if she’s training for a marathon, tracking her stress cycles, or just wants hard data to justify why she feels like garbage, the Oura Ring 5 is the most stylish health tracker out there. Packed with advanced sensors, it monitors heart rate, skin temperature, sleep quality, and stress levels. It's also one of the only wearables that can reliably predict my menstrual cycle. Plus, it works with both Android and iOS, so she’s not locked into a single tech ecosystem.

The BrüMate Togosa gets it. It’s a wine chiller, pitcher, or whatever you need it to be because we no longer have the patience for single-purpose objects. Slide in a prechilled bottle, twist the lid shut, and let the BevGuard triple insulation keep your drink icy without ice, condensation, or a watery demise. When the vibe shifts from pinot to sangria, swap out the chiller lid and pour in your batch of whatever (up to 49 ounces). The leakproof strainer lid also keeps fruit, ice, and other garnishes from pouring through. And because being checked out of Earth doesn’t mean trashing it, its lids are made from 13 recycled water bottles, some finishes are dishwasher-safe to conserve water usage, and the vessel itself is built to last a lifetime. (If for some reason it doesn’t, BrüMate also offers a lifetime warranty.).

She may not be able to move to another planet, but she can build a 3D model of the Milky Way from the comfort of her home. This 3,000-ish piece LEGO set recreates the spiral galaxy, turning our jumbled universe into galactic home decor. The finished piece can be mounted on the wall as a daily reminder that Earth is just one of billions of planets we believe exist—surely, at least one of them has better men.

The Everywhere Tote is for the woman who is going where the universe takes her. It has everything one might need for far-flung travels: a 16-inch padded laptop sleeve, a handful of interior pockets, and a water-resistant nylon exterior for when you’re caught in an otherworldly atmospheric anomaly. Available in elemental shades like coast blue, sea green, and clay pink—it’s at home anywhere, from the gym to an impromptu odyssey. If she needs to jet off on a moment’s notice, it’s got a key clip, a trolley sleeve, and an exterior pocket for her wallet and passport. It also meets airlines’ personal item requirements.

Sometimes, the only way to check out is to beam yourself into another world, preferably one with juicier plotlines. This projector has 450 ISO lumens and 1080p resolution, with 4K support and color calibration. The gimbal stand tilts 165 degrees for projecting on walls, ceilings, or the back of an RV. The included hard-shell case is great for portability and easy storage. It runs for 2.5 hours on a single charge, and it's power bank-compatible, so you can watch from anywhere. Its AI-powered setup takes care of autofocus, screen fit, obstacle avoidance, and keystone correction, so she doesn't have to fiddle with settings with every tectonic shake. For more projectors, check out our guide.

Cozy Earth’s Bamboo Pajama Set is one of my favorite sets to wear on a lazy Sunday. The button-up pocketed design features chic contrast piping that lends a hotel-style aesthetic. They make me want to put on my LED mask, pick up my Kindle, and sip on sleepy girl mocktails until I doze off. Made from 95 percent bamboo viscose and 5 percent spandex, this knit blend is cooler and more breathable than cotton. Cozy Earth introduces latest colors and prints each season, though the lighter shades can be somewhat sheer. If your giftee is over 5 foot 7 inches, I recommend the tall inseam. Sizes range from XXS to XXXL.

These Speks Odds Silicone Fidget Magnets are here to help you survive your stay in the stress-stricken simulation. Each set comes with three palm-sized magnets, encased in soft, textured silicone, designed to keep your hands busy while your brain zones out. I can’t stop fiddling with them when I’m watching TV and during Zoom calls. I can’t risk losing them by taking them outside, so they’ve found a home on my desk.

Sources indicate that speks also sells starter kits and gift bundles packed with other fidget toys. I loved the Moon Jelly Gump Memory Gel Stress Ball, until I handed it to my boyfriend for five minutes and he popped it. Men ruin everything.

Recent findings suggest that walking home alone at night on this planet is an absolute nightmare. If she can’t teleport away from creeps, she can at least blast a 130-decibel siren and flashing strobe light in their direction. The Birdie is a small but mighty alarm that will (hopefully) deter attackers and alert anyone nearby for help.

Sources indicate that I’ve used the original model for over a year (see my thoughts in my guide to the Best Personal Safety Alarms), and it’s given me peace of mind whenever I’m walking solo. The Birdie+, which I have yet to test, adds some useful features like location sharing, emergency support, and even a fake call function for a quick exit strategy. Plus, it comes in the cutest patterns. My one caveat is that this wouldn't be my first choice for a birthday gift or Valentine's Day, as it's kind of a downer.

She’s carrying her team at work, her family, and the knowledge that a recession is potentially looming. Don’t make her carry her water bottle, too. WanderFull’s Hydrobags have a thick, comfortable strap that takes a little bit of the load off her shoulders and come in dozens of colors and materials (including a newly introduced clear stadium line), one of which is sure to match her vibe. All Hydrobags bags can hold any handle-less water bottle up to 11 inches tall and 3.5 inches in diameter and sport two pockets for her phone and cards. If you can’t redistribute the household labor, the least you could do is redistribute the weight of her emotional-support beverage. —Kat Merck.

Apple raised its prices this year, but who didn't? Well, now that Black Friday sale season is here, this is your best chance to cancel out those price hikes. That's why we're paying extra close attention to early Black Friday Apple deals.

It has been revealed that yes, Apple does do Black Friday, but not in the way you might expect. Shopping directly on Apple's website usually means getting a measly gift card for future purchases. The real way to find great deals? Looking at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and Target. Especially as Black Friday approaches (mark Nov. 27 in your calendar), retailers duke it out to see who can offer the best prices on AirPods, MacBooks, and iPads. Walmart and Amazon are infamous for outdoing each other by a single cent.

Usually, prices on Apple products drop to record lows during the hectic Black Friday weekend. However, especially good deals can also sell out quick. In my five years covering Black Friday at Mashable, I've seen many an AirPod Pro deal go out of stock before I could finish writing a 200-word story about the deal.

In a recent development, shopping early lets you score decent savings while avoiding the post-Thanksgiving chaos. So, how do you know what to buy, and what to save for Black Friday and Cyber Monday? That's where the expertise of the Mashable shopping team can be helpful.

Recent findings suggest that let's start with the very expensive elephant in the room. In June, Apple raised prices on MacBooks, Macs, iPads, the HomePod, Apple TVs, and even the Vision Pro headset, followed by iPhone price increases in September. With some prices rising by $200 or more, the likelihood of them falling to record lows is low. Instead, I research the market to identify products that have been at or near record lows over the past five months.

Sources indicate that I also took into account the frequency of deals. If, like the AirPods Pro 3, there's a $50 deal that's nearly always on, I don't necessarily consider that a deal worth highlighting. On the other hand, if an iPad is $100 off for the first time in a month, I'll include it and note its pricing history.

Sources indicate that finally, I considered our reviewers' first-hand experiences with these products. Most of the items in this guide have been hands-on tested by at least one person on the Mashable staff, and I prioritized Mashable award winners, choosing the best deals based on overall product performance and value.

With five hours of battery life per charge, an IP54 water- and dust-resistance rating, spatial audio for immersive listening, and voice isolation for calls, they're a great daily pair of earbuds. With no silicone ear tips, they're also ideal for folks who like the Apple experience, but prefer a semi-open ear design. A24 is having a great year at the box office. That could give HBO Max a streaming edge

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.
  • A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.
  • Recent findings suggest that the studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

Recent findings suggest that the studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the manufacturer's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

The company plans to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz mentioned on the manufacturer's earnings call earlier this month.

In a recent development, paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

It has been revealed that the earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be notable as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The manufacturer has stated it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world.

There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them.

Recent findings suggest that for almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a major thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps.

Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.”.

Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings.

“During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they stated. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional.

“Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.”.

In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose.

They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”.

Recent findings suggest that “Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes.

Industry observers note that she noted, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.”.

The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague.

Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide.

The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it stated meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing.

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention.

There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

With continuing violence against the Rohingya, the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely.

But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar.

Sources indicate that “We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” indicates Salma.

Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.
  • At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.
  • It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of problems from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of problems from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” noted Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun remarked. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over challenges from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to newly introduced heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he mentioned.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

Industry observers note that china thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”.

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Recent findings suggest that congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier mentioned he wanted to do.

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions.

Industry observers note that china is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an notable opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”.

CNN’s Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to upcoming data from the US Energy Information Administration.
  • In a recent development, most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs.
  • Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, Upcoming Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to upcoming data from the US Energy Information Administration.

In a recent development, most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, Upcoming Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

Recent findings suggest that what particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today.".

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," claims Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests.".

Industry observers note that the 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30.".

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," notes Brod.

Sources indicate that he is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an key step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have mentioned 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach.
  • The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
  • Industry observers note that reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach.

The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.

Industry observers note that reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.

The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.

But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “concerns such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.

“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this matter.”.

Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.

It has been revealed that myanmar’s presidential spokesperson mentioned on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.

Recent findings suggest that “When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”.

The US state department mentioned on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.

Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.

The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.

In Brussels, the EU stated Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.

“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson noted in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that “The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”.

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.

The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.

In a recent development, the ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.

Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

In a recent development, ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI fans waited more than a decade for a new installment of the best-selling video game of all time.
  • Now they've grown up and they're itching to not just play GTA 6; they're also eager to participate in the Grand Theft Auto discourse.
  • From the debate over killing or sparing a character named Arnold to cataloguing all the wildlife cameos to the game's hot soundtrack, GTA 6 is driving countless conversations amongst players, including teens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto VI fans waited more than a decade for a new installment of the best-selling video game of all time. That includes teens who were toddlers when the game's last chapter debuted.

Now they've grown up and they're itching to not just play GTA 6; they're also eager to participate in the Grand Theft Auto discourse.

From the debate over killing or sparing a character named Arnold to cataloguing all the wildlife cameos to the game's hot soundtrack, GTA 6 is driving countless conversations amongst players, including teens.

According to recent reports, but the game is rated 17+ and features adult content, including sex, strip clubs, drugs, graphic violence, and murder. So, many parents whose teens want to play GTA 6 will likely find themselves in the familiar yet tricky position of balancing their child's interests and social life with exposure to content they feel violates their family's values.

Dr. Brett Biller, a child psychologist at Hackensack University Medical Center, wants parents to know it's OK — even advisable, in his opinion — to say no to GTA 6.

In a recent development, biller has no problem with video games in general. In fact, he acknowledges how online interactive games can have benefits, like socializing with friends over play.

Ultimately, however, he believes exposing tweens and teens to GTA 6's hyperrealistic community violence is simply not worth it.

"The negative consequences can outweigh the positive impact," Biller states.

While research doesn't prove that video game violence causes aggressive behavior, Biller notes there's a correlation between between violence in the home and aggression. That makes Biller cautious about exposing kids and teens to violent video games.

Sources indicate that killing zombies, he notes, is much different than murdering human characters, and younger children don't consistently grasp the difference between fantasy and reality. Yet Biller says older teens can also struggle in this way, especially given the realism of GTA 6. Plus, the game may normalize community violence by putting a teen player in the shoes of a thief or killer.

Meanwhile, teens with a history of witnessing or experiencing violence who play GTA 6 may find it difficult to manage the game's stimuli and their feelings about the content, Biller adds.

Beyond concerns about violence, parents may say no because they understand how playing GTA 6 will affect their child's mood, sleep, and personality.

"We, as caregivers, are responsible for making decisions that are in the best interest of our children," Biller says.

He recommends parents who won't permit their teen to play GTA 6 validate their child's frustration or fears of being left out.

Parents can also model how peer pressure is real and hard, because they feel it when other adults let their teen play GTA 6.

Biller notes this conversation presents a good opportunity to help a teen understand that standing up for their principles isn't always easy. He suggests parents explore with their teen other activities they can do with friends instead of playing GTA 6.

While some parents might feel better about playing alongside their teen, instead of the teen playing with friends, Biller indicates this approach is a "double-edged sword" that requires care and vigilance.

On one hand, parents who co-play have ample chances to point out and discuss concerning content or themes with their teen. On the other, co-playing can model to a teen that violence is fun or not a substantial deal.

In more cases than not, Biller finds that parents use this approach when they don't feel confident saying no or to justify their own choices.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit organization that reviews and rates entertainment content, described GTA 6 as an "extremely mature crime game" for adults 18 and older.

According to recent reports, still, its review notes that only parents will know if their older teen is ready to play. Either way, Jasmine Hood Miller, director of family resources and content strategy for Common Sense Media, claims parents should talk to their teen about the game.

Topics for discussion can include what looks fun about GTA 6, how women are depicted in sex scenes and strip clubs, and whether they think they'd hurt people in the game, or have done so.

According to recent reports, "It can be uncomfortable to talk about some of those topics," Miller states. "But honestly, if your kid is not talking to you, they're talking to someone else.".

Sources indicate that miller adds that these conversations should feel low pressure and not like a lecture. Instead, Miller encourages parents to be curious and nonjudgemental.

If a teen plays or watches the game at a friend's house, even after their parent has noted no, Biller recommends better understanding the context and validating their teen's feelings.

According to recent reports, "Reward them for being honest," he states. "We want them to continue to be open with us." This smell startup indicates its AI nose is as good as a human’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in a lab near Newark Airport in Upcoming Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says.
  • In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in a lab near Newark Airport in Upcoming Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, indicates founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”.

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It notes its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture newly introduced scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Recent findings suggest that wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

It has been revealed that A lot of the tech giant’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

In a recent development, mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.).

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

It has been revealed that osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn't a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.”.

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker notes. “Smell is super complex. Context is very vital for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”.

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.

Recent findings suggest that for that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko indicates. "So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”.

This article has been updated with an additional comment from Alex Wiltschko.

#70534. Voyager 1 had a data outage when it hit one light day. It still does.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1028 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager 1 had a data outage when it hit one light day. It still does.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Voyager 1 pushed past the one light-day distance milestone, the 49-year-old probe actually hadn't sent any science or engineering information home for days.
  • Voyager 1 still beams a steady radio signal to Earth, which tells engineers the spacecraft is alive and its antenna still points at Earth.
  • Voyager 1 crossed the milestone at 5:16 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Voyager 1 pushed past the one light-day distance milestone, the 49-year-old probe actually hadn't sent any science or engineering information home for days.

The trouble started Nov. 14, and it hasn't let up. Voyager 1 still beams a steady radio signal to Earth, which tells engineers the spacecraft is alive and its antenna still points at Earth. But the signal carries no information about the probe's health or what its instruments are measuring, and engineers don't yet know why.

Voyager 1 crossed the milestone at 5:16 a.m. ET Nov. 18, about 16.1 billion miles away, according to NASA. No other human-made object has traveled so far. Because the probe's radio signal takes a full day to cross space, the team didn't get word until 5:16 a.m. ET Nov. 19, when a ground antenna near Madrid picked it up.

It has been revealed that NASA marked the achievement Thursday with an hourlong celebration at its Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California that may have overshadowed the problem. Panelists shared memories of the mission, the agency played a video from fans around the world, and astronaut Jessica Watkins aboard the International Space Station provided a recorded tribute. The host covered the data outage in two sentences before opening the floor to questions. Officials delved into the spacecraft's current condition only after a reporter asked how the spacecraft was doing.

Industry observers note that "We have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," remarked Suzanne Dodd, Voyager's project manager. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We at the moment don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently.".

In a recent development, the carrier signal is the basic radio wave a spacecraft sends out — the same kind of wave a radio station uses to carry music. Voyager 1 normally loads its data onto that wave in packaged blocks, called frames. Antennas on Earth have to find where each block starts before anyone can read it, and that step is called the frame sync. In other words, right now, engineers can tell the station is on the air, but all they get is dead air.

In a recent development, all is not lost. The signal at least demonstrates that the computer keeping Voyager 1 aimed at Earth is doing its job, and that the probe's antenna and transmitter still work. The trouble more likely sits in a different onboard computer, the one that collects readings from the instruments and other systems and packages them for the trip home.

According to recent reports, but, clearly, fixing it won't be fast. Every command engineers send takes two days to produce an answer, the reality that comes with achieving the light-day milestone. NASA warned that finding the cause could take weeks or longer.

According to recent reports, the team indicates it has seen something like this before. In 2023, Voyager 1 also sent a carrier signal with no data. Engineers traced that problem to one of its onboard computers, and NASA said that experience is guiding their troubleshooting efforts. Engineers are also checking whether the outage connects to an episode in October, when the mission lost all contact with Voyager 1 for about 48 hours before the spacecraft reconnected on its own.

Sources indicate that if the team feared the outage might be permanent, it didn't show at Thursday's event. Panelists spent most of the hour smiling and reminiscing. When the problem came up, they treated it as routine.

It has been revealed that "The anomalies have become normal for us," said Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager's mission manager, who later added: "An engineer with a problem is like a dog with a bone. So we are very busy and very energized to solve these problems.".

Age makes everything harder. The original commands were sent on punch cards, Badaruddin remarked, and the team now has to make modern equipment talk to that 1970s hardware. Power keeps shrinking, too. Both Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, run on generators that turn heat from decaying plutonium into electricity, and each probe loses about four watts a year. To save energy, engineers have shut off instruments over the years. Voyager 1 now runs just two: a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields, and a plasma wave instrument, which picks up waves in the thin, electrically charged gas of interstellar space.

Sources indicate that this summer, engineers tried a risky move and successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 while replacing them with lower-power alternatives that still keep its fuel from freezing. The team expects the savings to keep the probe's instruments running until at least the 50th launch anniversary next summer.

Dodd compared the spacecraft to an aging human who takes longer to bounce back.

"All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things," Dodd said. "I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back.".

Voyager 2 remains healthy with three instruments working. NASA has noted it expects to lose both spacecraft eventually to problems engineers can't fix. But until then, the team will keep searching for workarounds like this summer's power swap.

"We pulled a rabbit out of a hat," Badaruddin remarked. "If we can find some more rabbits, we'll keep doing this.".
