#70533. Best Laptops for Travel (2026): Which to Take on the Road

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2101 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Best Laptops for Travel (2026): Which to Take on the Road

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as a laptop reviewer, I have plenty of devices to choose from when I travel for work.
  • Fortunately, there are many great travel laptops, and you’ll still appreciate them when you aren’t on the road.
  • Sources indicate that if there’s an obvious pick for the best travel laptop, it’s the Dell XPS 13.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as a laptop reviewer, I have plenty of devices to choose from when I travel for work. In some cases, my favorite overall laptop doesn’t translate into the one I want to travel with. When I’m squeezed into a plane, I’ll choose maximum battery life and portability over features like a bigger screen or more ports.

Fortunately, there are many great travel laptops, and you’ll still appreciate them when you aren’t on the road. Of the hundreds of laptops I’ve tested in my life, here are the ones I always choose to travel with.

Sources indicate that if there’s an obvious pick for the best travel laptop, it’s the Dell XPS 13. It’s been the best compact laptop you can buy for years, and that’s even more true in its latest incarnation. The key dimension to pay attention to on the XPS 13 is the depth, which is crucial for air travel. At 7.9 inches, it’s among the smallest laptops you can buy. Those economy-class seat-back tray tables on airplanes are only around 10 inches deep, and while that’s technically enough to accommodate even a 16-inch MacBook Pro, whether you can actually open the lid and use the laptop is another question. The XPS 13 is even smaller than the MacBook Neo, despite having a larger screen.

According to recent reports, the XPS 13 achieves this by using a 13.4-inch display (measured diagonally), compared to many of the 14-inch laptops on this list. Second, it has very narrow bezels around that screen, minimizing the device’s overall footprint. While 14-inch laptops have become more popular in recent years, that bigger display size also increases the overall footprint—and every millimeter counts when working on a plane. The XPS 13 still has enough room for your palms when typing (unless you have huge hands), and the keyboard is among my favorites to type on.

The other two major advantages for travel are weight and battery life. This little laptop only weighs 2.2 pounds, a full half-pound lighter than the 13-inch MacBook Air. You might forget you have it in your backpack while traveling.

According to recent reports, now, the XPS 13 isn't the most powerful laptop in the world—at least not the cheaper models. The standard version comes with only 8 GB of RAM and an Intel chip with only two Performance cores. It’s good enough for basic web tasks, but for real work, you might run into limitations. You can address this by opting for the 16 GB model (which keeps the price under $1,000) or upgrading to the much more powerful Core Ultra 7 355 processor. The latter is much more expensive and comes with twice the storage, but it doesn’t add extra weight or size. Regardless of the chip you choose, the XPS 13 gets absolutely fantastic battery life. It depends on what you're doing with it, but you could easily work through a long international flight without worrying about plugging in.

According to recent reports, if weight is your primary concern, the Asus Zenbook A14 is another contender. Despite being larger overall than the XPS 13 (with a bigger screen), the Zenbook A14 weighs 2.16 pounds—a hair lighter than the Dell. That’s seriously impressive, and I still remember how astounded I was when I first picked it up. Asus debuts its “ceraluminum” material in the chassis, which gives you the sturdiness of aluminum with the lightness of plastic. It’s not quite as rigid as metal, but it’s not as flimsy as ultra-light laptops in the past.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re less worried about working on the plane and more about lugging a laptop around, the Zenbook A14 is a good choice. The Zenbook A14 has several advantages over the XPS 13 that can be helpful on the go, including built-in ports like a headphone jack, USB-A, and HDMI. If you’re working out of a remote office or presenting to a client, these can definitely come in handy. The XPS 13 only has two USB-C ports and nothing else.

Recent findings suggest that there are a number of different versions of the Asus Zenbook A14 floating around out there. I’d stay away from the 8 GB model Asus sells and opt for the 16 GB model instead. There’s also a newer model that uses the Snapdragon X2 Elite chip, but I don’t think it’s worth the extra $450—especially not for a laptop focused on travel.

It has been revealed that the 13-inch MacBook Air also makes a great travel laptop. It’s relatively small, thanks to its 13.6-inch screen.

According to recent reports, in terms of portability, its main advantage over the XPS 13 and Zenbook A14 is its thinness. At 0.42 inches, it’s the thinnest laptop out there—and it doesn’t stick huge rubber feet on the bottom to compensate like other laptops do, such as the Razer Blade 14. You might not think thickness matters much in a travel laptop, but if you’re squeezing stuff into a backpack, every extra millimeter matters.

The MacBook Neo is also worth mentioning here. It’s not quite as thin as the MacBook Air, but because its screen is 0.4 inches smaller, it has a more compact overall footprint. Battery life is the bigger issue when taking the Neo on a trip, as it doesn’t last as long as the MacBook Air or Dell XPS 13. The 8 GB of RAM limitation doesn’t affect its use as a travel laptop much, but it's something to consider for a work laptop in general. That said, it has a very pretty screen for a laptop at this price.

It has been revealed that budget laptops aren’t typically known for being particularly lightweight and travel-worthy. Most of them struggle, especially with battery life. The HP OmniBook 5 might be an exception. You can usually find it on sale for under $700, even with 16 GB of RAM and an OLED display.

In a recent development, the OmniBook 5 isn’t quite as compact as the MacBook Neo because of its larger screen, but it is also half an inch thick and weighs only 2.8 pounds. The Snapdragon X Plus also delivers solid battery life, plenty to feel comfortable traveling with. It’s not a laptop without compromises (like the poor touchpad), but it comes with 16 GB of RAM, unlike some other laptops at this price. That’s a solid deal if you need something to travel with on a budget.

Sources indicate that good question. Tablets can make for great travel devices because of their size and ease of use. If you need a proper keyboard and touchpad—and the app support to handle a typical workday—you’re probably better off getting a laptop.

The Surface Pro 12 is the two-in-one laptop I’d recommend first. It’s absolutely tiny for a computer, even though it runs the full version of Windows 11. Even with the detachable keyboard connected, it weighs only 1.8 pounds. The only real problem with bringing this on a plane is the kickstand, which adds some extra depth. It’s just small enough that it should fit while open on an airplane tray table, unlike the 13.8-inch Surface Pro model.

Recent findings suggest that of course, that kickstand is also a huge advantage for the Surface Pro 12 if you’re using it without the keyboard. While that would make work difficult, it’s ideal for watching movies. Set this up on your tray table with some movies downloaded, and you’ll be the envy of your aisle. And when you need to get some work done in a coffee shop or at a smaller table, you’ll be happy to have access to the keyboard and touchpad—both of which are very comfortable to use. Just know that it's sold separately.

Sources indicate that the iPad Air, paired with the Magic Keyboard, avoids the Surface Pro 12’s kickstand glitch. And with only an 11-inch screen, it’s perfect for use in small spaces—with or without the keyboard (note that there is also a 13-inch version). If you can accomplish all your work on an iPad, more power to ya! The iPad Air should give you everything you need, so long as you get the Magic Keyboard. If your travels involve more leisurely activities, the iPad Air is a great device for reading by the pool or for playing games.

According to recent reports, one benefit of this latest version of the iPad Air is not only its performance (thanks to the M4 chip inside) but also the front-facing camera, which has been moved to landscape for more natural-feeling video calls. Of course, you could also opt for the 11-inch iPad Pro for extra performance (and the incredible tandem OLED screen). It’s also slightly thinner and lighter, though I don't think it's worth the significant price difference.

Lastly, there’s definitely room here for laptops with 360-degree hinges—a different class of two-in-one laptops. I haven’t tested a recent Windows device with this form factor that I truly loved, but there’s no question it works well on an airplane. Just fold the screen back with the keyboard face down, and you have the perfect screen for watching movies. The Lenovo Yoga 9i 14 is a gorgeous option, though it’s incredibly expensive right now. But if you can afford it, you’ll love the 2-in-1 action combined with one of the slickest designs imaginable. The Framework Laptop 12 is also worth considering. While it’s a bit thick and heavy for a travel laptop, its smaller screen, touchscreen, and 360-degree hinge make it a good option. It’s also one of the cheaper options available, and it’s user-upgradeable.

What to Look For in a Travel Laptop.

Whether you’re packing for a trip across the world or across the state, a proper travel laptop shouldn’t be heavy or overly large. That rules out 15-inch and 16-inch laptops, which are so big you can’t use them on airplane tray tables or at coffee shops. But even when you narrow it down to 14-inch laptops or smaller, there are three portability factors to consider.

When you’re on the go, you want a laptop that doesn’t constantly make you worry about finding an outlet. Bringing a laptop power bank can help, but the biggest factor in staying sane while traveling is a device that can stay on. Many factors affect how long a laptop can last, including CPU efficiency, battery wattage, screen brightness and resolution, and more.

Long-lasting laptops, such as the Dell XPS 13, will get you through a long flight. The processor is the main thing to look out for. Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X series of chips are battery-efficient, as are Apple’s M-series chips. Intel also has some highly efficient CPUs in its most recent lineup, though you’ll need to pay close attention to the model number, as it can vary wildly depending on the specific CPU you’re using. To dig deeper, read my extensive guide on How to Buy the Right Laptop, which breaks down different CPU options.

How Large Are Airplane Tray Tables.

Industry observers note that the size of seat-back tray tables varies. There’s no exact size because of various factors, such as the airline, aircraft, cabin, and seat. Remember: Just because a laptop can physically fit on a tray table doesn’t mean you’ll have space to open and use it. With that in mind, here are the general averages to keep in mind. Airlines do not list tray table sizes, but you can expect one in economy to measure around 16 x 9 inches, while premium cabins will have larger tables depending on the seat.

It has been revealed that I’ve included both tablets and laptops in my recommendations, but your choice will depend on why you’re traveling with a device. If it’s for a vacation and you really only need a device to read, watch, and play on (perhaps with the occasional email check), a tablet works perfectly. Lounging with a tablet, whether on a plane or by the pool, feels much more leisurely than using a laptop. More importantly, it'll help you avoid dipping back into work mode. Whether an Android tablet, iPad, or Windows tablet, just pair it with a compatible keyboard case—and you’re good to go.

Sources indicate that however, if you’re traveling for work (or need to work while traveling), a proper laptop will be better. The one you already have may work just fine, but frequent fliers know they prefer a more compact device. And more specifically, a small laptop with a keyboard and trackpad will work better on your lap or on small desks than a tablet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen.

An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in Newly introduced York ⁠City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy ⁠to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the ​235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal ‌court.

The discovery of alleged ‌assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has ‌denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in Upcoming York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who ‌was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.

Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear ​whether he has hired a defense lawyer.

India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley ⁠Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices ​in this country, ever.”.

Addressing the ​court on Friday, Gupta noted ​he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

“I’m ​sorry to Mr ‌Pannun, I’m sorry ​to the communities I hurt, ​I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta mentioned.

Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.

“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

According to recent reports, the balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source remarked, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person stated, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical upcoming insights to the People’s Republic of China.”.

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have noted.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it states is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

According to recent reports, CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the latest intelligence.

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official noted in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”.

According to recent reports, gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, stated at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”.

It has been revealed that the surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Sources indicate that still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Alex Marquardt contributed to this report.

#70526. Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1295 w)

Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • Recent findings suggest that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

Recent findings suggest that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

It has been revealed that apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

According to recent reports, it's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," said Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Industry observers note that fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves rapidly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out new garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

"We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," stated U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

According to recent reports, the average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," stated Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

Though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

Industry observers note that sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She mentioned that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

"There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman stated. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

Nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

Apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, mentioned BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

"Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," mentioned Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, noted China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

"They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," said Lu.

Industry observers note that alixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," said BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also remarked she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

Ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the company said it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

In a recent development, the brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Industry observers note that alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

It has been revealed that shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the firm is doing well.

It has been revealed that "What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," stated AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes.
  • Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
  • In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes.

Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.

In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

The international court of justice (ICJ) mentioned it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.

Recent findings suggest that for months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.

Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.

Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.

Sources indicate that rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.

Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.

Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.

It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.

In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.

Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.

Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.

When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.

She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.

Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.

To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.

According to recent reports, elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.

His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

It has been revealed that alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

Industry observers note that french President Emmanuel Macron on Friday described Russia's actions in Ukraine and Europe as an "irresponsible gamble" that would only increase European resolve. "By escalating its war of aggression against Ukraine and also pursuing an aggressive agenda on European soil, Russia is making an irresponsible gamble that can only further isolate it and strengthen the resolve and unity of Europeans, and of all those who want to work towards peace and stability on our continent," he wrote on X.

Denmark meanwhile accused Russia of attempting to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper on its soil.

US President Donald Trump has defended his admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin while deflecting a reporter's question as to whether the Russian strongman is a friend to the United States or just the president.

In a recent development, "I can't speak to America" but stated: "I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with]. It's actually very good.".

Trump said the two bonded over the 2016 US presidential election, which Democrats say involved Russian meddling on Trump's behalf, charges that Trump rejects as what he has branded the "Russia hoax.".

The US leader also said it will be hard to end the war in Ukraine — something he said he would easily do on his first day back in office nearly two years ago — because of the animosity between Putin and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

#70520. The Boox Picco made me love tiny e-readers

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (807 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

The Boox Picco made me love tiny e-readers

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I don't get the hype of tiny e-readers.
  • Recent findings suggest that boox is one of the first big brands to launch a mini e-reader of its own, the Picco.
  • Industry observers note that the physical design of the Boox Picco isn't all that different from other tiny e-readers, but what matters is literally what's on the inside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I don't get the hype of tiny e-readers. I've used a ton of e-readers — Kindles, Kobos, and Boox — and I thought they were just the right size, and I wasn't craving a smaller e-reader. But plenty of people clearly are, as I've spent hours browsing Reddit and reading about how people use their tiny e-readers.

Recent findings suggest that boox is one of the first big brands to launch a mini e-reader of its own, the Picco. Other Boox e-readers run on Android, but the Picco does not. I expected to be underwhelmed, but I'm glad to be wrong. The Boox Picco has given me a whole latest love for tiny e-readers, and I finally understand their appeal.

Industry observers note that the physical design of the Boox Picco isn't all that different from other tiny e-readers, but what matters is literally what's on the inside. The user interface is exceptionally easy to navigate and straightforward — it's pretty pared back compared to Kindle or Kobo.

In a recent development, the Picco combines physical buttons and touchscreen controls. The 'bookshelf' section is the device's native library. 'Transfer' lets you move books from the Boox Tile app on your phone to the device; 'Apps' offers a limited selection of pre-downloaded apps; and 'Settings' is exactly as it indicates. You can even set any photo as your lock screen, but keep in mind that the Boox Picco display is black-and-white only.

You can easily move to the home screen by swiping up, and swipe down to adjust brightness and warmth. Plus, it has two side buttons, which serve as page-turn buttons. The Pico is super responsive and loads pages swiftly. I was worried I'd get overwhelmed by all the controls, but it's so intuitive that I quickly took to it and was navigating like it was second nature.

There isn't much to navigate on the device, but that's part of what makes it so easy. It's all about keeping you focused with apps like a to-do list and a Pomodoro timer.

According to recent reports, if you've used other e-readers, you might be used to devices from the same brand speaking to each other. So Boox e-reader consumers might expect the Picco to sync with other Boox models. Unfortunately, that's not the case. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

In a recent development, the Boox Picco only connects to WiFi temporarily to transfer files. Since it doesn't maintain a connection, it won't frequently enhancement to reflect whatever's in your Boox library. This also means that it won't update your progress in a book across e-readers, so you'll have to manually turn the page to catch up when you switch devices.

In a recent development, with a 3.97-inch screen, it's an incredibly small e-reader designed to literally fit on the back of your phone. While other tiny e-readers have promised the same, the Boox Picco really does. Its MagSafe case is perfectly positioned so it attaches conveniently without hanging off the side. Keep in mind, though, it fits best on an iPhone Pro Max (pictured below).

In a recent development, it feels very sturdy, too, living up to its $110 price tag. Weighing two ounces, it has a slight heft so it doesn't feel like it'll slip out of your hand, but it also doesn't add too much weight to your phone when attached.

Tiny e-readers have one massive overarching concern, so this isn't exclusive to the Boox Picco, but you're only able to read DRM-free EPUB files. Typically, these e-books are only in the public domain, so you're extremely limited in what you can read on the device. That means any EPUBs you borrowed on Libby or purchased on Kindle or Kobo can't be uploaded to the Boox Picco.

So, for most e-reader users, the Boox Picco won't align with their reading habits.

Recent findings suggest that yes, the Boox Picco is the tiny e-reader worth buying — although it won't be for everyone. You need to temper your expectations about what you can read on it, as it only supports DRM-free EPUBs. But if you're reading DRM-free EPUBs on your e-reader anyway, then the Boox Picco is a fun device to add to your repertoire.

According to recent reports, it's well-designed inside and out, with a sturdy case that snaps onto MagSafe devices, and an easy-to-navigate user interface. At $109.99, it's cheaper than most e-readers we've tested, which feels on par for a device that is smaller and possesses fewer capabilities than a standard e-reader. And if you're deciding between an Xteink e-reader and the Boox Picco — go for the Picco. It's far more user-friendly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attorney general says E1 settlement decision should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu.

Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, mentioned any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever newly introduced administration was formed.

She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

Recent findings suggest that the deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.

It has been revealed that eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”.

The EI settlement expansion, due to have been declared on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.

Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.

According to recent reports, the construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.

Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.

Bennett mentioned: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”.

Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related problems, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.

If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.

The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing.

Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an key step, but the struggle is not over yet.”.

Latest Update: What a billion-dollar deal notes about the US battery market

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.
  • Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
  • Sources indicate that this arrangement also demonstrates how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

Sources indicate that this arrangement also demonstrates how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this upcoming material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

In a recent development, we’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the organization when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

In a recent development, the tech giant opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky claims, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

Industry observers note that this agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a massive one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Recent findings suggest that sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.).

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the organization holds decarbonization as a priority.

According to recent reports, “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he mentioned. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our firm. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”.

According to recent reports, pretty much everyone: If Amazon is pretty intrinsic to your spending, then going for a Kindle, specifically the Paperwhite Signature Edition, makes the most sense. According to recent reports, the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition dethrones the 2024 Kindle Paperwhite as the best overall e-reader. Historically, I've preferred the Paperwhite, finding that the Signature Edition doesn't have enough features to justify its price, but the 2026 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition finally fixes that. With a fresh aluminum case, the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition feels like a high-end piece of tech. With a thinner body and square edges, this new Kindle feels more like a smartphone or tablet than it does an e-reader.

According to recent reports, but inside the more advanced chassis is still the same e-reader you love. It's fast with a high-contrast 300 ppi resolution. Read our full review of the Kobo Clara Colour.

It has been revealed that for those who want an Amazon alternative: If you're just diving into the world of e-readers and not particularly thrilled about Kindles and their Amazon ties, then the Kobo Clara is the right answer. It offers a color display for those who enjoy manga and graphic novels, but it remains speedy with fast processing when turning pages or swapping between books.

Libby users: It's especially great for Libby users, who want seamless integration with books that automatically load into your library as soon as you borrow them. While Kindle's Libby integration only works in the U.S., the Kobo works with Libby no matter where you live.

In a recent development, having tried my hand at more than a dozen e-readers in all shapes, sizes, and brands, I wasn't expecting to be so deeply impressed by the Kobo Clara Colour, but it is a wonderful e-reader. With a 6-inch screen, it's slightly smaller than the Kindle Paperwhite, but it allows you to hold it comfortably for multiple hours at a time without any wrist or arm fatigue.

In my previous testing with Kobo devices, I've really liked them, but one sticking point is that they're slower than Kindles. Initially, I found that the Kobo Clara kept up with the Paperwhite, but after several months of use, it had a tendency to lag. Compared to Kindles, I had to manually sync the Kobo Clara to get my library books to show up.

Its processing system is otherwise really smart and fixes one of my biggest e-reader pet peeves. When you adjust the font size on a Kindle, the device doesn't recalculate how many pages are in the book, making it inaccurate, so you don't know exactly how many pages you have left in a chapter. The Kobo Clara does recalculate page count accurately for a more exact reading experience. Though, one thing to note: Kobo counts the number of digital pages, whereas Kindle page numbers typically match up with physical book copies.

For the same price as the Kindle Paperwhite, the Kobo Clara offers color displays, something you can't get in the Kindle lineup unless you're willing to spend $250. The colors aren't as bright as you'd experience in a physical book, but they're still vivid enough to enjoy a graphic novel.

The Kobo Clara's biggest downfall is its battery life. It's supposed to last up to 42 days, although many online owners say it averages out at about two weeks. That's quite pathetic in the face of the Kindle's 12-week battery life; however, I'd trade in a better reading experience over a couple weeks of battery life any day.

Read our full review of the Durobo Krono.

Across app readers: If your digital library is sprawling — you have books through Kindle, Kobo, Libby, and Audible — then you need an e-reader that can access all of them. Durobo's Krono e-reader is a compact e-reader that basically functions like a tablet. Most e-readers on this list are Androids, but none have open Android systems that let you download the apps you want, as the Krono does.

Audiobook lovers: For the audiobook lovers, the Durobo Krono also plays audio in addition to transcribing it. With access to the Google Play store available, you can download any app you read on to access your digital library, including Audible, Libro.fm, and Spotify. However, if you have a collection of EPUB files, you can also download them directly to Krono's library.

It has been revealed that having tried several other open Android e-readers, I haven't been impressed. The Remarkable Paper Pro is way too big and the Boox Go is too slow and too difficult to get books on, so I wasn't expecting much from the Durobo Krono. Turns out, it is a phenomenal e-reader.

Since I test e-readers for a living, my digital library is spread out across all different platforms. Rather than balancing a bunch of different e-readers, the Krono puts both my Kindle and Kobo libraries on one device. The only library I don't have access to is Apple Books, since it's unavailable in the Google Play Store.

The Durobo Krono is the perfect size, with a 6.13-inch display, similar to the basic Kindle. It has a matte display with 300 ppi resolution. It also has a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth.

Powered by an octa-core processor, it moves quickly between apps and books. It easily competed with the speed of both Kindles and Kobos; however, it can get bogged down. It runs the Kindle app, Libby, and Libro.fm no problem. But some apps, like Substack, slowed it down with their high internet demands. Once I deleted the Substack app, though, it got back to normal.

As someone who loves to read while listening to the audiobook, I also love that I can do both on one device. I can listen to an audiobook on Audible while reading the EPUB file alongside it. The Krono also has voice transcription and note-taking capabilities, a nice bonus feature, but not essential in an e-reader.

Because it can tackle a lot of apps rather than just doing one thing like a Kindle, it needs some extra power behind it. Unfortunately, it doesn't quite have it. The Boox Go 6 suffers from significant lag and screen response issues that make it occasionally frustrating to use. It's slower than either a Kindle or a Kobo, but it's a consolation you'll have to make if you want an e-reader that does more.

Miniature enthusiasts: If you want an e-reader that you can have on you at all times and even slip in your pocket, there are so few options out there. That's what makes the Xetink X4 so special. It's a truly tiny e-reader with a 4.3-inch display; but with a built-in magnet, it can attach to MagSafe devices so you can keep it attached to your iPhone.

Sources indicate that you must love DRM ePUBs: If you think you're getting a mini Kindle, you're not. Instead, expect a tiny e-reader that is a great fit for turning online articles into PDFs or collecting all the free ePUBs. It's not compatible with any DRM files.

Industry observers note that in such a little package, the Xetink X4 feels like it should be a toy, but it's actually a solid e-reader. It's the smallest e-reader we've tested, measuring 4.3 inches, so you can slip it in your pocket and go. That small display, while convenient on the go, won't be suitable for all eyes, especially if you like to crank up the text size on your e-reader or phone.

It has been revealed that the resolution of the Xetink X4 is 219 ppi, which is lower res than you'll find on most e-readers. It also includes page-turning buttons along the bottom of the e-reader. Xteink has a great transfer system, too. It's similar to Amazon's Send to Kindle feature, in that you can send EPUBs and articles to the e-reader. The ability to send articles is particularly compelling, so you can send your reading list to your e-reader and enjoy them in one spot.

My biggest issue with the Xetink X4 is how few files it supports, as you can't access Libby books or any DRM files on it. However, folks at Lifehacker figured out how to install different firmware onto the device for a better reading experience.

While the color display on the Kobo is nice, it is still rather muted. While reading Heartstopper, the colors were quite toned down in comparison to how they appeared on the iPad Mini. Plus, it's a bit slower than a Kindle, with the occasional stall while switching between books.

While the Kindle may have the Kobo beat on processing and battery life, I still think the Libra Colour is a worthy upgrade as it offers the best design of an e-reader with the perk of color. Amazon's color e-reader, the Colorsoft, costs $289.99, so at $259.99, the Libra is a little cheaper.

According to recent reports, young readers: If you're raising a voracious reader, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is the best e-reader for kids. It's waterproof, which means it stands up to juice spills and dips in the pool. Plus, it comes with a built-in case. It's designed to be kid-proof, not just physically, but also with built-in parental controls. If you're concerned about monitoring your kid's bookshelf, this Kindle allows you to approve downloads by kids and displays age-friendly titles that kids can easily access.

In a recent development, one area where Amazon has all other e-reader brands beat is in the kids market. There are special kid-friendly models of the basic Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, and Kindle Colorsoft. Our preferred model for kids is the Kindle Paperwhite Kids.

Recent findings suggest that more than anything else, an e-reader for kids has to be waterproof, which is why the Kindle Paperwhite Kids is the best choice. It comes with everything we like about the standard Paperwhite: a beautiful, high-resolution screen that works faster than any previous generation.

It has been revealed that but what makes it great for kids is that it's a distraction-free device. It doesn't come with ads, notifications, or the temptation of games or video. I also like that it's a bit heavier than the standard Paperwhite, giving it a sturdier design. Plus, the built-in case adds an extra level of protection.

According to recent reports, the parental controls are easy to use and set up, and the device also comes with a six-month free subscription to Amazon Kids+, which provides unlimited access to thousands of age-appropriate books. The library of books is easy for kids to navigate and offers classics like Lois Lowry's The Giver and modern classics like Diary of a Wimpy Kid.

What I don't love is the price. At $229.99, it's more expensive than the standard Paperwhite. If you want to go for a budget kids' pick, I'd recommend the standard Kindle, which you can set up as a kids' device during setup to ensure parental controls and add an Amazon Kids+ subscription for $5.99 per month. Plus, as your kid ages, you won't have to upgrade to a more teen-friendly e-reader.

Read our full review of the Kindle Scribe (3rd Generation).

In a recent development, for annotators and journalers: If, looking through your bookshelf, your books have dog-eared pages, highlighted lines, and scribbles in the margins, your instinct might be that an e-reader isn't for you, but I'd like to introduce you to the Kindle Scribe. It's the only Kindle with writing capabilities and comes with an included stylus pen that magnetically attaches to the side of the e-reader; it's ready for all your handwritten thoughts.

Industry observers note that the pen moves nicely across the screen, mimicking the texture of writing on paper. In addition to a library of books, the Kindle Scribe also comes with a journal section where you can take notes. The notes feature is especially great for students who want to handwrite notes and convert their handwriting into text.

Industry observers note that the 2025 Kindle Scribe got a much-needed upgrade. All the good stuff has held over with the addition of some major improvements.

Recent findings suggest that it's still big, with an 11-inch display, which does make it a little more awkward to hold while reading, but for writing or annotating, it's optimal. Unlike other tablets (I'm looking at you, iPads) that require you to buy a pen separately, the Kindle Scribe comes with a pen that conveniently attaches to the side so it doesn't get lost. However, it's not the most secure magnetic hold, so be careful not to bump the pen off accidentally.

Writing on the Kindle Scribe is a joy. Before testing this e-reader, I used my iPad and Apple Pencil to annotate readings, but I never loved it because the screen felt too slick for the Apple Pencil. The Kindle Scribe does not suffer this problem, as the matte screen lends some friction to the pen, making it feel like you're writing on paper. I enjoyed writing with the pen, and I swear my handwriting looked better on the Kindle Scribe than on my iPad.

It finally got a processing upgrade that makes it as speedy as every other Kindle. Gone is the lag when switching between journals and books. Plus, the displays have greatly improved, too, as the 2025 Kindle Scribe has virtually no ghosting. Like the Kindle Paperwhite, the Scribe's battery life lasts 12 weeks. It also has storage options, with 32GB and 64GB versions available.

It has been revealed that it's not your only option if you want a Kindle that can write. The Scribe Colorsoft is also available, and while we appreciate that model, it's quite a bit more expensive. The 2025 Scribe is a better value; it just doesn't have the wow factor of color.

Read our full review of the Apple iPad mini.

Single device consumers: There are so many devices that the modern person is meant to have. If adding an e-reader seems superfluous, I'd recommend a tablet that allows you to read books, stream shows, and browse the internet. The best tablet for reading? It's the iPad mini.

It has been revealed that but why is this iPad better than any other? It's all about the size. At 8.3 inches, it comfortably sits in your hand and is about the same size as a paperback.

Sources indicate that before testing these e-readers, I read using my 9th-generation iPad, and my main complaint was always the size. After 30 minutes of reading, my hand and wrist would strain holding up all 10.2 inches of the screen. That's why the 8.3-inch display of the iPad mini was such a treat. Reading with the mini made me feel like I was holding an actual book rather than a laptop screen.

Unsurprisingly, the iPad mini has the most computing power of all the e-readers on this list. It jumps between apps and turns pages without an ounce of hesitation. Plus, it offers the most expansive ways to read books. You can read using Apple's built-in Apple Books app or download and read within the Kindle and Libby apps. And unlike most e-readers, you can read comics and graphic novels in full color. Plus, it has far more storage than any other e-reader, as the 7th generation iPad mini starts at 128GB of storage.

Despite my love of the iPad mini, I have some beef, most of which is with the screen. While I love its overall size, it has a substantial glare problem. I've found this to be true with any iPad I've read on; the slick glass screen has a glare in almost any environment. That's no surprise in the sun, but even at night, I found the screen to be a little too shiny, causing my eyes to have some trouble focusing. This does have a fix; if you want your iPad screen to look more like the matte of a Kindle, a screen protector such as Paperlike creates that effect.

Additionally, compared to e-readers, which provide months of battery life, the iPad mini only gets you hours. If you're reading for a couple of hours a day, you're probably only charging the iPad once a week, which isn't a massive deal but certainly more than a traditional e-reader.

Topics Amazon Books iPad Kindle E-Readers.

According to recent reports, when picking an e-reader, price is always a consideration. However, almost all e-readers fall into the same price range. Kindle and Kobo e-readers both start around $149.99/$159.99, while the tiny Boox Picco is just $109.99. If you want handwriting capabilities, Kobo and Boox make the most affordable options, as Kindle's Scribes start at $500.

Remarkable PaperPro: Whenever you search for e-readers, Remarkable's tablets will always pop up in the search results, but unfortunately, it's hard to obtain ePUB files on the Remarkable. With Remarkable, you can access files within Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive. If you have any locked ePUB files — like from Libby — you won't be able to access them on a Remarkable tablet. So, after testing the Remarkable tablet myself, it proved to be a better document reader or digital journal than an e-reader.

Recent findings suggest that onyx Boox Go 7: While we love the Boox Go 6, we didn't love the Go 7. It's the same size as the Kobo Libra or Amazon Kindle, but it really lags on processing speed. Reading ePUB files from Libby required downloading the Adobe Digital Editions app onto the Boox Go 7, and there was significant lag when opening and closing the app. While it was an easier process than getting library books on a Nook, it was still a major pain compared to Kindle or Kobo's integrations. The Boox Go 7 lagged and took ages to load files. I was most looking forward to testing this Boox because of its page-turning buttons, but unfortunately, I found that they didn't work on my device.

Recent findings suggest that boox Palma 2: I loved reading on the Boox Palma. It's a really solid palm-sized e-reader with an open Android system, so you can download any reading app from the Google Play store, including Libby, Kindle, and Kobo. Unfortunately, the Palma 2 is being discontinued, and its availability is dwindling, which is why it's not included in this list.

In terms of big-name e-readers, you might notice one omission from this list: the Barnes & Noble Nook. I have tested this e-reader, and it was previously featured on this list. However, after testing more devices, it no longer makes the cut. In comparison to any of the Kindles or the Kobo Libra, the Nook has sloth-like performance, making it frustrating to use.

Sources indicate that plus, getting my library books onto the Nook was a nightmare, as it was a multi-step process that required downloading to a computer before uploading to a Nook. Its only redeeming quality was the buttons on either side of the device, which made page turning a breeze. However, unless you are a loyal buyer of Barnes & Noble books, I recommend steering clear of the Nook.

Recent findings suggest that once you get an e-reader, it's time to fill it up with books, and that doesn't necessarily mean spending money. In fact, you can load up your e-reader without spending a dime; you just need to be a bit resourceful.

The best way to read nearly any book — a classic or hot new release — is with Libby. I have read hundreds of free books with the Libby app — I wouldn't have been able to test for this guide without it. It connects with your library card, allowing you to borrow from your local library's digital collection. Plus, both Kobo and Kindle have exceptional Libby integrations.

Industry observers note that another way to build your library is through Stuff Your Kindle Day events. These are 24-hour opportunities led by authors that make books discounted or free.

If you're a fan of the classics or looking to discover a treasure lost to time, an online resource like Project Gutenberg has more than 75,000 books in the public domain that you can download and read on an e-reader.

The best Kindle is the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, dethroning the standard Paperwhite. Overall, it strikes the right balance of performance and value, while possessing everything we want in an e-reader. The standard Kindle is great for those on a budget, but it's not waterproof, and while the basic Paperwhite is always a favorite, the Signature Edition aluminum case and extra features make it the best e-reader you can buy.

Industry observers note that our two favorite e-readers come from Kindle and Kobo, but is one better than the other? It depends on what you're looking for. If performance is your primary concern, then a Kindle, specifically the Paperwhite, is better as it outperforms the Kobo Libra Colour in terms of speed when turning pages or loading books. However the Kobo Clara Colour measures up to the Paperwhite's performance.

According to recent reports, if you're looking to de-Amazon your life, then a Kobo e-reader is the better e-reader. It offers all the things we like in a Kindle, such as Libby integration, adjustable brightness and warmth, a waterproof rating, and an overall better-designed package. While Amazon discontinued its Kindle Oasis, an e-reader with page-turning buttons, the Kobo Libra Colour has not abandoned this fan-favorite design. It also features an internal gyroscope so you can rotate the Kobo for a better ergonomic experience.

It has been revealed that yes, you can read on an iPad, and as an iPad reader, I highly recommend it. iPads come with the Apple Books app. However, other reading apps, including Libby and the Kindle app, give access to the world of books.

It has been revealed that for this reason, I included an iPad in my testing. The iPad Mini made my list because it is the perfect size to feel like you're reading a paperback novel versus larger iPad models like the 9th generation, which feel like reading a clunky magazine.

According to recent reports, buying an e-reader is a far more significant investment than going to the bookstore. Plus, you still have to buy e-books. At first glance, it seems like an expensive adventure. Luckily, even with an e-reader, you can support your local library. With Libby, you can borrow and read audio and e-books from your local library and get them on your digital e-reader.

Libby has an iOS app and can instantly send books to your Kindle. If you don't happen to have a Kindle or iPad, you can still upload your library books through Adobe Digital Edition. Aka, you can still support your local library — and not pay a single penny to read a new book.

I tested each of these e-readers over several weeks, reading at least one book per device in different environments. Here are the criteria upon which we decided this guide.

How easy was it to download and read new books from Libby or the Amazon store? Did the Scribe's stylus work smoothly? Is the user interface intuitive or was there a learning curve? I also noted which e-readers work best with Libby, for easy access to library books.

E-reader models vary wildly in price; I made sure to include affordable options as well as splurge-worthy models that are a good value.

This includes auto-adjusting displays for indoor/outdoor reading, warm light settings to block blue light, note-taking abilities, and page turn buttons for one-handed reading.

I made sure to pinpoint which models are waterproof for a worry-free outdoor reading experience as well as those better suited for children.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Below, you can review a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany from Friday, November 20:.

Representatives of IG Metall, Germany's largest union, mentioned Friday that thousands of union workers at dozens of factories around the country will continue to carry out 24-hour strikes in an effort to force employers to cough up a 5% wage increase as well as job guarantees.

Audi, BMW, Ford, Opel and Volkswagen are all in IG Metall's sights, as are shipyards in northern Germany.

Companies say they cannot afford to pay wage increases and will have to slash benefits, site upgrades and hundreds of thousands of jobs in the automotive, electrical and mechanical engineering and metal production sectors.

They are instead offering a phased increase of 1.3% for 2028 — Germany's current inflation rate is hovering around 3%.

It is the first time the union and its 3.7 million members have turned to 24-hour strikes in eight years and they are hoping the move will offer them some leverage when collective bargaining talks begin next week.

It has been revealed that IG Metall's northern coastal representative Daniel Friedrich noted Friday: "Our members stand united behind our demands. On Monday, we will continue the 24-hour strikes at more companies.".

Police in the German state of Saxony say they deployed water cannons to Leipzig and used them on individuals who repeatedly shot fireworks at officers there after a large demonstration ended.

Police say roughly 2,500 people took part in a demonstration in Leipzig organized by the group Gen Z Takes Charge, far fewer than the estimated 7,000 who joined the first of these on October 31 (see entries below).

Across Germany, some 87,000 people joined in demonstrations, according to Gen Z Takes Charge.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in latest German defense and technology investments.

During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz stated, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation.".

The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to new partnerships in the defense industry.".

That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.

The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.

The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace.".

Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations.".

Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.

He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.

The German broadcaster Sky TV — not to be confused with the British-based Sky Sports F1 which is the largest English-language commercial F1 broadcaster — will not be sending any staff to the Formula 1 Qatar Grand Prix because of security concerns in connection with the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East.

Sky TV announced the move on Friday, just a week before the contentious race weekend from November 27-29.

Sky will broadcast the entire race weekend as usual, but will use global feed images and will not send any of its own staff to Lusail International Circuit.

F1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia this spring were canceled as the US war with Iran was in its most active phase, with major disruptions to commercial flights.

The season-ending double header in Qatar and then the United Arab Emirates a week later has been in serious doubt ever since.

Nominally at least, both races are going ahead — and in all likelihood, teams will have already started dispatching equipment and personnel to the region to begin preparations by now.

Sky TV noted it still planned to send a team to the season finale in Abu Dhabi, just across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, on December 6.

But it said it continued to "monitor developments and assess the situation on an ongoing basis.".

Organizers of the Gen Z Takes Charge protest group spoke out about why they took to the streets again.

Co-organizer Akram Selo called on Germany's leadership to meet the young people's demands.

"Talks won't make us stop demonstrating," he told RBB-Inforadio in comments aired on Friday.

Industry observers note that "Essentially, our demands should be addressed, and we should be given assurances. That is what needs to happen, not empty promises," Selo added.

In a recent development, "So far, we feel that we aren't being taken seriously at all," he mentioned. "The way we're being treated suggests that the aim is to sideline our demands and discriminate against us by focusing on other trivial matters.".

Another group, the alliance "School strike against conscription" held its own protest to demand an immediate halt to surveys about potential availability for the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, that are right now non-binding and only obligatory for teenage boys.
