AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
  • Recent findings suggest that the report is an upgrade to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used.
  • The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

Recent findings suggest that the report is an upgrade to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot demonstrated that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

Sources indicate that it’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

Recent findings suggest that and AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the organization (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

According to recent reports, METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

According to recent reports, though it’s difficult to score these fresh tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”.

Kapoor states he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor indicates. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the latest report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

In a recent development, but because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” notes Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”.

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, indicates that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”.

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

Recent findings suggest that in the latest report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how swiftly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”.

Industry News: A Space Probe Returns to Asteroids Where NASA Tested Planetary Defense Systems

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage.
  • Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth.
  • In a recent development, in the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

Astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

In a recent development, in the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely key link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

In a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a massive space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA rolled out the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

According to recent reports, scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

In a recent development, but questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

But of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

Hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an crucial detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

Sources indicate that the probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

Industry observers note that according to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras.
  • Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they mentioned was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.
  • According to recent reports, the brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras.

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they mentioned was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

According to recent reports, the brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

In a recent development, zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He mentioned the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor mentioned that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.

The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.

She noted the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”.

The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an vital moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, mentioned while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”.

He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”.

Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”.

Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.

Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

  • UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers.
  • "Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts stated in a statement in mid-November.
  • They remarked that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.

"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts stated in a statement in mid-November.

They remarked that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests.

A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.

"There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.

Sources indicate that in October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests. Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.

Industry observers note that "The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators," remarked Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers.".

Recent findings suggest that even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prizeafter being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

According to recent reports, yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.

Industry observers note that criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.

Yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure, for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.

According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he said, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this.".

Shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.

"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired.".

In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.

Industry observers note that "This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior.".

Industry observers note that moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.

It has been revealed that referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour mentioned: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect.".

However, Moinipour stressed that, despite this pressure, "many lawyers in Iran continue to defend the rights of their clients and accept the risk of arrest, criminal prosecution, and professional restrictions. In doing so, they are prepared, if necessary, to pay a high price for this resistance.".
